sections.html:
On the Mississippi side of the state line, Southaven is a DeSoto County city roughly 14 miles south of downtown Memphis. As a principal city of Greater Memphis, it has many owners who work, shop and fly out of Tennessee yet pay their taxes in Mississippi. Residents numbered 54,648 in 2020 and an estimated 57,493 in 2024, which ranks Southaven third in Mississippi and first among Memphis suburbs.

The city covers about 41.5 square miles. Interstate 55, which also carries the I-69 designation, runs north to south through it, with U.S. 51 and Mississippi Highway 302 as other main roads. The airport at Memphis International lies about two miles north of the city's center point, with approach paths from both north-south runways running right over town. Noise questions from buyers are common.

Incorporation came in 1980, after Memphis homebuilder Kemmons Wilson laid out subdivisions of small starter homes just across the state line. In the years that followed, the city doubled its land area while its population tripled. Southaven Towne Center opened in October 2007 and Tanger Outlets Southaven in November 2015. Because homes went up over several decades, repair needs differ from street to street, and a seller usually hears about them from the buyer's inspection report. A house that struggles through inspection is where an as-is cash sale often comes up.

Long hot summers, frequent rain and past storm damage push roofs and drainage to the top of most inspection reports, so walk the property with those in mind. Nearly 55 inches of rain fall in a year, with April the wettest month, and an EF-2 tornado touched down in Southaven on February 5, 2008.

  • Roofs: look for lifted shingles and granule loss after storm seasons.
  • Drainage: standing water near the slab or crawl space often shows up in inspections.
  • HVAC: long cooling seasons put heavy wear on air conditioners.

Plenty of Southaven households have a Tennessee job, doctor or school connection. When you sell, remember that the house, the tax bill and the deed are all in Mississippi, so Mississippi rules apply even if your agent, lawyer or lender is across the line. Confirm that whoever handles your closing is comfortable with DeSoto County recording and tax practices. Ask for a written list of what you will owe at the table, including any tax balance, so the numbers hold no surprises on signing day.

The county mails the bill. It covers the preceding assessment year, is due February 1, with the next Monday accepted without penalty or interest when the first lands on a weekend or holiday.

The state formula counts 10 percent of true value for a house its owner lives in and 15 percent for any other real property, a rental included. County, city and school district each set a millage rate, and all three apply to the assessed value. A bigger bill can come from a higher value, a higher rate, or both.

  • Pay in person at the Tax Collector's offices in Hernando, Olive Branch or Horn Lake, by mail, or online.
  • The DeSoto County Tax Collector's number is 662-469-8030.
  • Tax sale day is the last Monday in August, with bidding handled on an online platform run with GovEase.

A parcel sold at tax sale has a clouded title, and that generally must be cleared before you can close. Ask the DeSoto office how redemption works on your parcel before you rely on it.

If you dispute an assessment, the Chancery Clerk can explain how to get a Board of Supervisors hearing, which is normally requested by the first Monday in August.

Your exemption stays with you. The next owner has to file with the county Tax Assessor from January 1 to April 1, because it is never automatic. The filer needs to own the house and live there as a primary residence on January 1, and the deed has to be on file at the Chancery Clerk before January 7. That timing leaves a spring buyer waiting for the next tax year, while a December closer can still apply.

A missed filing or an income tax problem can cost the exemption. A seller who also owns a second house should check that only one property carries it.

Southaven's Building Department issues permits and examines plans, and its phone number is 662-393-4639. A homeowner may submit the building permit for their own home but must hire a contractor holding a Mississippi state license for trade work.

Did a project stall halfway? Call the Building Department before you list or take an offer and find out whether a permit is still open, because unfinished permitted work can hold up a sale.

An agent, a sale by owner and a cash buyer each suit a different Southaven seller. Listing is sensible for a well-kept house and a seller who can outwait showings and financing. Selling by owner saves the commission, yet every form and negotiation lands on your desk. Cash is quickest and comes with no repair requests.

When an inspector turns up problems, you cut the price, pay for repairs or lose the buyer. A direct as-is sale removes that fork in the road. Ask any buyer to put the offer in writing, and keep the paperwork you have been given.

An empty Southaven house still produces bills. Property tax, insurance, utilities and lawn care continue each month whether or not a buyer shows up, and a long listing period adds up. Stack those carrying costs against the gap between listing and cash prices, and ask what a few extra months would truly cost.

Mississippi Code section 89-1-503 obliges the seller to deliver the written property condition disclosure statement ahead of the title transfer. If the statement comes after an offer, the buyer can cancel within three days of hand delivery or five of mailing.

A cash sale as is leaves that duty in place and only changes who pays for repairs. Cash Home Buyers works with Southaven sellers who would rather sell the house in its present condition than manage contractors, and we explain the terms in writing before anyone commits.

Even so, the closing path is familiar: a title search surfaces liens and unpaid taxes, they are paid from your proceeds, you sign the deed, and the Chancery Clerk records it. Take photo ID, tax receipts, permit records and, for any mortgage, a payoff letter. Because no lender is involved on the buyer's side, the appraisal and loan approval stages do not slow the date.

faqs.q: Can I sell a house in Southaven, MS without making repairs?
faqs.a: Yes. Nothing in Mississippi law demands repairs first, though the written property condition disclosure statement still goes to the buyer. As-is buyers reduce their price for repairs.

faqs.q: When are DeSoto County property taxes due?
faqs.a: February 1 covers the preceding assessment year. A weekend or holiday date moves the deadline to the next Monday.

faqs.q: When does DeSoto County hold its tax sale?
faqs.a: Every year on the last Monday in August, with bidding done online.

faqs.q: Does the buyer keep my homestead exemption?
faqs.a: No. Each new owner files separately during the January 1 to April 1 window, and has to own and live in the home on January 1 of the tax year.

faqs.q: Who do I call about a building permit in Southaven?
faqs.a: Call the Building Department on 662-393-4639. You may file the permit for your own home, though trade work needs a contractor holding a Mississippi state license.
